prompt: Could you write a captivating short story beginning with the sentence: The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.
answer:
The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.

On the morning before its demolition, it began returning things.

A red mitten appeared on Mrs. Bell’s doorstep. A wedding ring rolled out of a kitchen tap. Mr. Alvarez found his childhood dog waiting beside his bed, young again and smelling of rain.

By noon, everyone in town was pretending very hard that nothing unusual had happened.

Then a paper airplane landed at Ada’s feet.

She knew its crooked wings. She had folded them herself, twenty-three years ago.

Inside, in her brother’s handwriting, were five words:

*You still owe me one.*

Ada sat down on the pavement.

Ben had been nine when he disappeared. She had been twelve. They had been daring each other to approach the abandoned house, and she had called him a coward.

He had gone through the front door.

He had never come out.

The police searched every room. Her father tore up the cellar floor. Nobody found so much as a shoe.

Now Ada picked up the airplane and walked to the end of the street.

The front door opened before she knocked.

Inside, the house smelled of pencil shavings and wet wool. Shelves covered the walls, crowded with spectacles, single earrings, keys, photographs. Somewhere, a kettle whistled.

“Ben?”

A young boy leaned over the upstairs banister.

“You took ages.”

He wore the same yellow jumper. There was still a scab on his chin.

Ada gripped the newel post.

Ben’s smile faded. “You look like Mum.”

She climbed the stairs slowly, frightened that any sudden movement might scatter him.

“How long have you been here?”

“Since yesterday. I think.”

He looked toward a window. Beyond it was another room, and beyond that another, stretching away in warm, dusty light.

“It gets confusing.”

Downstairs, something heavy struck the floor.

A grandfather clock had appeared in the hallway.

“The house is emptying,” Ben said. “It’s been doing that all morning.”

Ada reached him. His hand was warm.

For a moment she could do nothing except hold it.

Then she pulled him toward the stairs.

At the front door, his fingers slipped through hers.

Ada turned.

Ben stood several feet behind her, staring at his hand.

“I’ve tried that,” he whispered.

Words had appeared on the door, scratched into the wood.

**ONLY WHAT IS LOST MAY BE RETURNED.**

“He is lost,” Ada said.

The house creaked.

On a nearby shelf stood a blue biscuit tin. Ada recognized that too: their mother had kept Ben’s treasures in it after the search ended.

She opened it.

Marbles. A plastic astronaut. A photograph of Ben with his two front teeth missing.

Underneath lay the death certificate issued seven years after his disappearance.

Ada understood.

They had stopped looking for a lost boy. They had begun mourning a dead one.

She took out the certificate and tore it in half.

Nothing happened.

Behind her, Ben began to cry quietly.

Of course nothing happened. She remembered the funeral without a coffin. Their father’s empty chair at Christmas. Every birthday she had calculated the age Ben would never reach.

A piece of paper could not undo all that.

Outside, an engine started.

Ada knelt before her brother.

“I don’t know how to do this,” she said.

He wiped his face on his sleeve. She used to scold him for that.

Then he glanced at the airplane sticking out of her coat pocket.

“You still owe me a dare.”

Ada looked at the open doorway.

Beyond it waited a street where she had spent most of her life without him.

She held out her hand.

“Bet you can’t beat me to the gate.”

Ben hesitated.

Then he ran.

Ada ran after him, through the doorway and down the steps, and caught him just as he reached the pavement.

Behind them, the house gave a long, settling sigh.

Ben looked up at her, breathless.

“I won.”

For the first time in twenty-three years, Ada laughed.

“Yes,” she said, holding him tightly. “You did.”
